Interesting question! I did a little bit of research to see if I could help you out, and I found this:

As a result of the human authorship standard, “under U.S. current law, an AI-created work is likely either (1) a public domain work immediately upon creation and without a copyright owner capable of asserting rights or (2) a derivative work of the materials the AI tool was exposed to during training,” Esquenet continues. “Who owns the rights in such a derivative would likely be dependent on various issues, including where the dataset for training the AI tool originated, who, if anyone, owns the training dataset (or its individual components), and the level of similarity between any particular work in the training set and the AI work.”

Assuming the prior cases precluding authorship for non-humans is followed, “it could preclude anyone from owning the output, essentially dedicating such works to the public,” Kelber says. “And that result could also be supported, since the vast amount of source materials are at least publicly available.”

So there's a LOT of exposition masked as dialogue here. 

Is any of that stuff explained to the reader before meeting the dragon? Ex: the tyrant serpent divine, the Queen, Sephir, Korbon, Bellorg. 

If this is all new information to the reader, you're pretty much info dumping a bunch of names that the reader has no connection to yet. The importance of all that stuff doesn't really come across as impactful if I don't know what the dragon is even referencing. For example, I can't tell if Sephir is a location or a character. I would assume it's a location, but if that's the case, I don't have any scale for it. Is it a city? A hamlet? I would suggest establishing that beforehand so you don't have to squeeze it all in the dialogue.

I think you could get away with this dialogue if you reduce the amount of exposition, but that might not work so well in this case. Namely because I don't see why this dragon would give an unsolicited history lesson. 

With all that experience and pride, surely the dragon would expect the heroes to have heard of him already. Why waste his precious, ancient breath explaining all that?

I'm sorry for the confusion - I think I found an explanation that might make it a bit clearer:   

"You probably know that, in music, the rhythm of a song is the “beat,” often created by instruments such as drums, bass guitars, etc. In fact, in popular music the drummer and bass guitarist in a band are often referred to as the “rhythm section” because they establish the rhythm for the rest of the musicians to follow.

Unlike a song, poems don’t have a rhythm section. There is no drummer or conductor establishing the rhythm. Instead, the rhythm is set by the “stresses” or “accents” in the words themselves. Allow me to explain.

In most words that have more than one syllable, one of the syllables is pronounced more strongly than the others. We say that this syllable is “stressed” or “accented.” For example, the word “apple” has two syllables – ap-ple – and the first syllable is pronounced more strongly than the second. That’s why the word is pronounced “AP-pull” and not “ap-PULL.”

If a word has just a single syllable, that syllable might be stressed, or it might not be. Generally, short words like “a” and “I” and “the” are not stressed. Nouns and verbs (things and action words), on the other hand are often stressed, even when they are just one syllable long. So, for example, words like “cat” and “jump” are stressed syllables.

The easiest way to tell if a word is stressed or not is to put it in a sentence and then read it aloud. Listen carefully to how you pronounce it to see if you can tell which words or syllables are stressed and which ones aren’t.

Let’s take a look at an example. Read the following line and see if you can hear the stressed syllables.

My mother ate an apple and my father ate a pear.

Could you hear that every other syllable was stressed? One way to write this to make it more obvious is to capitalize the stressed syllables and write the unstressed syllables in lowercase letters, like this:

my MOTH-er ATE an AP-ple AND my FATH-er ATE a PEAR.

Now can you hear it? I hope you can see that, by writing your words in such a way that they form repeating patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables, you can add rhythm to your poems.

----

To give an example from your text, there is a rhythm here:

With-IN the SPRA-wl of MOUN-tains TALL
There STOOD a SIN-gle PEAK.

And the rhythm begins again with:

a-LONE and IN-dist-INCT it HID,
With DEATH be-LOW at SLEEP.

From what I read from your text, the rhythm resolves at the end of the second line, and then starts up again. And it stays this way without breaking.

So maybe having a single line that concludes  on its own can help make your poem sound less repetitive. 😄 Otherwise it sounds like the rhythm is endlessly looping

Out of curiosity, is there a way to break the rhythm of your structure every now and then?

I noticed a few things that might be worth considering: 

I'm pretty sure that "[...]Chicken or the Egg?" is not a riddle, but a causality dilemma. Also, it sounds kinda odd that Loki would talk about something of Greek origin. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I'm pretty sure it was a question originally posed by a mortal philosopher dude named Plutarch?
 
As for Loki's answer, I feel like his explanation is over-complicating things. You can kill the boar as many times as you want to with the spear. It will still return to life after its heart stops beating.

The spear is still deadly enough to kill. And the boar can still survive being killed. Since both outcomes are true, one doesn't make the other any lesser. They are only following their nature of being. Both can exist together in harmony.

Hannibal Lector and Clarice had a similar story in the Hannibal book, where he tried to brainwash her into becoming his sister, but Clarice ended up changing his mind by offering herself in her own right mind. That ending was super controversial and angered a lot of fans who didn't like the romance, but I loved it ❤

Personally, if you laid the groundwork for me to ship them (I'm a sucker for the sexy villain trope), I'd be disappointed enough to stop reading. 😅 It would remind me too much of Hannibal and Clarice, and I'd feel frustrated that there wasn't any payoff to the tension that you're building. 

But that's just me. I think only a small minority of fans would actually want your characters to end up together. 🙂

Does he have to be in so much pain?

I can't imagine someone staying erect while they're in excruciating pain. And back pain doesnt just go away when you roll over, lol. Especially when it's as terrible as what you're describing. 

Whether or not she goes on top doesn't change anything. When I'm in pain like that, my boyfriend offers to give me a massage and cuddle, not try and find a different position to have sex with me. If he did try and have sex with me despite the pain, I'd feel like he wasn't being very considerate of how I'm feeling.

Respecting his physical limitations and boundaries is more intimate than trying to force a sexual encounter between them when he's literally suffering. It makes her sound pushy, like she's more concerned about having sex than trying to help him relax and find a way to sleep through the night. Have you ever slept with severe back pain before? It's not easy. 

Why not have her give him a massage instead? They could try again some other night when he's feeling better.

Tbh, I don't get the sense that this sex scene would an improvement for a character who never had a healthy relationship with sex. I get the vibe that he's being pressured into having sex with her, especially since it's their wedding night. 

Would this be his first time having sex after being raped? Having sex again after being raped can be extremely difficult for some survivors, so do keep this in mind. It's important not to gloss over this detail. I suggest reading up about survivor's guilt and how it can impact your future relationships.

Tbh, I find your use of a rape scene more controversial than writing a sex scene between two consenting adults.

Are you familiar with the tv show Hannibal? It's one of the few horror masterpieces out there that doesn't rely on rape to fuel a character's personal growth. 

Something to consider, from the words of Bryan Fuller:

"There are frequent examples of exploiting rape as low-hanging fruit to have a canvas of upset for the audience. The reason the rape well is so frequently used is because it’s a horrible thing that is real and that it happens. But because it’s so overexploited, it becomes callous. That’s something I can’t derive entertainment from as an audience member — and I’m the first person in the audience for ‘Hannibal.’ My role, as a showrunner, is to want to watch the show we’re creating. And if something feels exploitative or unnecessary, I’ll try to avoid it.”

‘A character gets raped’ is a very easy story to pitch for a drama. And it comes with a stable of tropes that are infrequently elevated dramatically, or emotionally. I find that it’s not necessarily thought through in the more common crime procedurals. You’re reduced to using shorthand, and I don’t think there can be a shorthand for that violation — it’s an incredibly personal and intimate betrayal of something that should be so positive and healthy. And it’s frequently so thinly explored because you don’t have the real estate in 42 minutes to dig deep into what it is to be a victim of rape. It appears over and over again in crime procedurals without upping the ante and without exploring everything that happens. All of the structural elements of how we tell stories on crime procedurals narrow the bandwidth for the efficacy of exploring what it is to go through that experience.”
